statement: In a triangle, one angle measures 30 degrees. Of the other two angles, one is exactly twice the other. What is the largest angle in the triangle?

choices.misconception: I found the smaller of the two unknown angles and stopped before doubling it.
I split the remaining 150 degrees into two equal halves instead of a one-to-two split.
I split the remainder evenly into 75 and 75, then doubled one of them.
I assumed that the largest angle in a triangle like this must be a right angle.

hints: The three angles add to 180 degrees, so the two unknown ones add to 150.
Call the smaller unknown angle x. Then the other is 2x, and x + 2x = 150.
3x = 150, so x = 50 and 2x = 100. The angles are 30, 50 and 100, which sum to 180.

solutions.reliable: The angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees, so the two unknown angles together make 180 - 30 = 150. Writing the smaller as x makes the larger 2x, so x + 2x = 3x = 150 and x = 50. The two unknown angles are therefore 50 and 100, and the largest angle in the triangle is 100 degrees. Check: 30 + 50 + 100 = 180. The transferable idea: naming the smaller share x keeps an uneven split from collapsing into an even one.
solutions.elegant: The remainder of 150 splits into three equal shares of 50; the larger angle takes two of them, giving 100.

whyOnTest: Naming the smaller quantity x is what keeps a one-to-two split from collapsing into an even one.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
